pos: n. (a case for a corpse; the Egyptian sarcophagus that held Joseph's body)
etymology: From Greek kophinos, a basket, through Old French cofin, a chest. The KJV uses it once, at Genesis 50:26, for the Egyptian aron that held Joseph — the same Hebrew word later used of the ark of the covenant.
biblical_def: Genesis ends not with a burial but with a box waiting to be moved: “So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt” (Genesis 50:26). Everything about the sentence is Egyptian — the embalming, the sarcophagus, the country — and Joseph had arranged that none of it would be final: “And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence” (Genesis 50:25). The coffin was a claim on a promise. For roughly four centuries it sat in Egypt as a standing witness that this was not home. Exodus records that the claim was honoured on the night of the deliverance: “And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you” (Exodus 13:19). And Joshua records the end of the journey, in ground bought by Jacob generations before: “And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver: and it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph” (Joshua 24:32). Hebrews 11 counts the instruction about the bones, not the governorship, as Joseph's act of faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a coffin as the chest or box in which a dead human body is buried, or deposited in a vault; and notes the older sense of a basket or case.
webster_full: COFFIN, n. [Gr. a basket; Fr. coffin.] The chest or box in which a dead human body is buried, or deposited in a vault.
COFFIN, v.t. To put into or enclose in a coffin.
EMBALM, v.t. To open a dead body, take out the intestines, and fill their place with odoriferous and desiccative spices and drugs, to prevent its putrefaction.
BONE, n. [Sax. ban.] A firm hard substance, of a dull white color, composing the skeleton of an animal body.
SEPULCHRE, n. [L. sepulchrum.] A grave; a tomb; the place in which the dead body of a human being is interred.
scriptures: Genesis 50:26
So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
Genesis 50:25
And Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you, and ye shall carry up my bones from hence.
Exodus 13:19
And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him: for he had straitly sworn the children of Israel, saying, God will surely visit you; and ye shall carry up my bones away hence with you.
Joshua 24:32

And the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, buried they in Shechem, in a parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for an hundred pieces of silver: and it became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
corruption_summary: Christian burial is refashioned as a celebration of a life, and the body — which Scripture treats as the thing to be raised — becomes an inconvenience to be disposed of quietly.
corruption_paragraphs: Joseph's coffin is an argument about bodies. He could have been buried with honour in Egypt's finest ground, and he refused, because the body that would rise belonged in the land of the promise. The modern funeral increasingly reverses this: the casket is absent, the remains are handled offstage, and the service is arranged around memories of a personality. Scripture is stubbornly physical. It counts bones, buys graves, records burial plots by the acre, and calls death a sleep from which the body wakes.

The doctrine at issue is the resurrection of the body, which the 1689 confesses along with every historic creed: the selfsame bodies, and none other, raised with different qualities. A burial practice that treats the body as a discarded shell is preaching a different anthropology — nearer to Plato than to Genesis. This is not a rule about caskets or cremation, on which Scripture gives no command; it is about what a Christian funeral says. Hebrews 11:22 singles out Joseph's instruction concerning his bones as the act of faith worth recording from a whole life of remarkable ones.
roots_summary: Hebrew aron (H727), a chest, ark, coffin; etsem (H6106), bone; chanat (H2590), to embalm, spice.
roots_lines: Hebrew aron (H727) — a chest; the same noun used of the ark of the covenant, Exodus 25:10.
Hebrew chanat (H2590) — to embalm, to ripen with spices; Genesis 50:2 and 26.
Hebrew etsem (H6106) — bone; the object of the oath, carried out of Egypt.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, attend to; God will surely visit you, the promise the coffin held.
Greek ostea (G3747) — bones; Hebrews 11:22, Joseph's commandment concerning them.
usage: “Put in a coffin in Egypt” — Genesis ends with a box that has not arrived.
“Ye shall carry up my bones” — a claim laid on a promise.
“Buried they in Shechem” — four centuries later, in ground already bought.

pos: n. (a vessel for drawing water; the measure Isaiah sets against the nations)
etymology: From Old French buquet, a tub, akin to Old English buc, a pitcher. In Scripture the bucket appears twice, and both times it is a figure — once for a nation's overflowing prosperity, once for the weight of all nations before God.
biblical_def: Balaam, compelled to bless where he was hired to curse, reaches for the most ordinary thing in a village to say that Israel will not run dry: “He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted” (Numbers 24:7). Isaiah takes the same vessel and uses it for the opposite weighing: “Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing” (Isaiah 40:15). Not a bucket, a drop from one — the film left on the rim that no one bothers to shake off. That is the empires, weighed. The bucket appears again at a well in Samaria, where the woman raises the only objection that occurs to her: “The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?” (John 4:11). She is right about the vessel and wrong about the Man. And Jeremiah names the alternative to drawing from God: “For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bucket as a vessel in which water is drawn out of a well — made of leather, wood, or iron.
webster_full: BUCKET, n. [Sax. buc, a pitcher.] A vessel in which water is drawn out of a well; it is nearly in the form of a pail.
BUCKET, n. A vessel for drawing up water from a well, or for holding water, as in a fire-engine.
CISTERN, n. [L. cisterna.] An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor, as in domestic uses, distilleries and breweries.
BALANCE, n. [L. bilanx.] A pair of scales, for ascertaining the weight of bodies.
DRAW, v.t. To pull along; to haul; to cause to move forward by force; to take water from a well.
scriptures: Numbers 24:7
He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted.
Isaiah 40:15
Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing.
John 4:11
The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?
Jeremiah 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 40:15 is quoted as though it made human affairs meaningless, when the chapter's point is comfort — the God who weighs empires so lightly carries His lambs in His bosom.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse is pastoral. A believer frightened by the news is told that nations are a drop of a bucket, and hears that nothing matters. Isaiah 40 was written to exiles under the largest empire then alive, and the chapter that weighs the nations at a drop ends with mounting up with wings as eagles. The principle to recover is that the smallness of empires before God is the ground of a Christian's courage, not of his indifference.

Jeremiah 2:13 names the alternative exactly, and it is the more useful verse for ordinary life. The two evils are one motion: forsaking the fountain, and then hewing out cisterns. A cistern is not a sin against good sense — it is a reasonable piece of engineering, and everyone in Judah had one. The sin is preferring stored water to running water, a supply a man controls to a supply he must go to God for. And the cisterns are broken, which is not the prophet's pessimism but simple observation about anything built to replace God.
roots_summary: Hebrew deli (H1805), a bucket, from dalah, to draw; mar (H4752), a drop; maqor (H4726), a fountain; bor (H953), a cistern.
roots_lines: Hebrew deli (H1805) — a bucket; from dalah, to draw up, Numbers 24:7.

Greek antlema (G502) — a vessel for drawing; John 4:11, nothing to draw with.

“A drop of a bucket” — not a bucket; the film left on the rim.
“Cisterns…that can hold no water” — the reasonable substitute that fails.

pos: n. (woven coverings; the same furnishing on two very different beds)
etymology: From Old French tapisserie, from Greek tapes, a carpet or rug. Proverbs uses it twice, for coverings a woman has made or bought — and the two women could not be further apart.
biblical_def: Proverbs puts the same furnishing in two houses and lets the reader weigh them. The strange woman advertises hers: “I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt” (Proverbs 7:16). Everything is imported, displayed, and offered to a young man who is passing in the street; the tapestry is bait, and the sentence is a sales pitch. The virtuous woman of the closing acrostic has the same article and never mentions it to anyone: “She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple” (Proverbs 31:22). Hers are made, not bought, and they come in a list of things done for her household: “She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet” (Proverbs 31:21). The contrast is not between luxury and austerity — both women have fine cloth, and the Bible never treats beauty in a house as a fault. The contrast is between covering used to seduce and covering used to keep a family warm. Jael's mantle belongs to the same family of weavings put to a purpose: “And Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said unto him, Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not. And when he had turned in unto her into the tent, she covered him with a mantle” (Judges 4:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tapestry as a kind of woven hangings of wool and silk, often enriched with gold and silver, representing figures — used for covering walls and furniture.
webster_full: TAPESTRY, n. [Fr. tapisserie, from tapis, carpet; Gr. a carpet.] A kind of woven hangings of wool and silk, often enriched with gold and silver, representing figures of men, animals, landscapes, &c.
TAPESTRY, v.t. To adorn with tapestry, or with hangings.
COVERING, n. That which covers; any thing spread or laid over another, whether for security or concealment.
SCARLET, n. A beautiful bright red color, brighter than crimson.
PURPLE, n. A color composed of red and blue blended; a color anciently the badge of rank and wealth.
scriptures: Proverbs 7:16
I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt.
Proverbs 31:22
She maketh herself coverings of tapestry; her clothing is silk and purple.
Proverbs 31:21
She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet.
Judges 4:18
And Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said unto him, Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not. And when he had turned in unto her into the tent, she covered him with a mantle.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 31 is read either as a rebuke of beauty and enterprise or as a checklist of feminine achievement, and the plain fact that the woman is richly furnished for her household's sake is missed both ways.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The two common misreadings are domestic. One treats Proverbs 31 as an austerity standard, so that a woman who furnishes her house well feels worldly; the text has her in silk and purple. The other turns the chapter into a performance review that no woman can pass. The principle to recover is that the acrostic is a portrait of wisdom housed, and every item in it — the fields, the merchandise, the scarlet, the tapestry — is aimed outward at a household and a city gate.

Set beside Proverbs 7 the point sharpens. The strange woman's inventory is identical in quality and opposite in direction. She lists her furnishings to a stranger; the virtuous woman's are noticed by the writer, not advertised by her. What Scripture judges is not the fineness of the cloth but who it is for. A house arranged as a display and a house arranged as a shelter can hold exactly the same goods, and Proverbs is careful to give them the same goods so the difference cannot be mistaken for a difference in income.

Hebrew argaman (H713) — purple; the dye of rank, also the tabernacle hangings, Exodus 26:1.

“She maketh herself coverings of tapestry” — made, and never mentioned by her.
“Not afraid of the snow for her household” — what the cloth is finally for.

pos: n. (an enclosure for sheep; the place David was taken from)
etymology: From sheep + cote, a small shelter or hut (Old English cote, a cottage). The KJV uses it for the rough field enclosure — a wall of stones, sometimes a cave — where a flock was penned at night.
biblical_def: Israel's greatest king is repeatedly identified by the place he was fetched from, and it was not a palace or a school. “He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70), and the next verse keeps the smell of the work in it: “From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance” (Psalm 78:71). The verb in both lines is God's — He chose, He took, He brought — and the training given was the care of pregnant ewes, which is to say the care of the weak and the slow, the exact skill a shepherd of Israel would need. The day of his anointing shows how little anyone else valued the post: “And Samuel said unto Jesse, Are here all thy children? And he said, There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep. And Samuel said unto Jesse, Send and fetch him: for we will not sit down till he come hither” (1 Samuel 16:11). His own father did not think to call him in. Later the sheepcote appears again as the setting of David's severest test: “And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave” (1 Samuel 24:3) — where the shepherd spared the king who hunted him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sheepcote as a small enclosure for sheep; a pen — from cote, a cottage, hut, or shed.
webster_full: SHEEPCOTE, n. A small inclosure for sheep; a pen.
COTE, n. A cot; a hut; a sheep-fold.
SHEEPFOLD, n. A place where sheep are collected or confined.
EWE, n. A female sheep; the female of the ovine race of animals.
SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture. In Scripture, one who exercises pastoral care over a flock.
scriptures: Psalm 78:70
He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds:
Psalm 78:71
From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.
1 Samuel 16:11

And Samuel said unto Jesse, Are here all thy children? And he said, There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep. And Samuel said unto Jesse, Send and fetch him: for we will not sit down till he come hither.
1 Samuel 24:3
And he came to the sheepcotes by the way, where was a cave; and Saul went in to cover his feet: and David and his men remained in the sides of the cave.
corruption_summary: The shepherd image is sentimentalized into gentleness, and the sheepcote — a hard, dirty, dangerous post — disappears from the picture of what pastoral care actually costs.
corruption_paragraphs: Every church window with a smiling shepherd and a clean lamb works against Psalm 78:71. The training was following ewes great with young — slow, filthy, night work in lambing season, at the mercy of weather and predators, for animals that cannot be reasoned with. That is what God chose as the apprenticeship for a king, and the New Testament keeps the word for elders. A man who wants the title of pastor and not the sheepcote has mistaken the office for a platform.

The second thing the sentimental picture loses is the sheepcote's danger to the shepherd himself. 1 Samuel 24 puts David in one, with Saul unarmed and asleep at the mouth of the cave, and his own men quoting providence at him to justify the kill. He cut a hem and his heart smote him. The sheepfold is where a man finds out whether he will take by force what God has already promised to give, and that test comes to anyone who has been anointed for something and made to wait for it.

Hebrew alah (H5763) — giving suck, great with young; the ewes David followed.
Hebrew raah (H7462) — to feed, tend, shepherd; used of David and of the LORD, Psalm 23:1.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to shepherd, tend; the charge given to Peter, John 21:16.

“Following the ewes great with young” — the apprenticeship for a throne.
“There remaineth yet the youngest” — his own father did not send for him.

pos: n. pl. (watering channels at a well; the gutters where the flocks came to drink)
etymology: From Old English trog, a hollowed vessel. In Scripture troughs stand beside wells, and they are where the flocks and the people meet — which is why so much of Genesis and Exodus happens at one.
biblical_def: The watering trough is a fixed feature of patriarchal life and, in Scripture, a place where God arranges meetings. Jacob works his years for Laban at one: “And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink” (Genesis 30:38), and again: “And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods” (Genesis 30:41). Much has been made of Jacob's rods as folk science; the account itself credits nothing to the sticks, and Jacob later tells his wives plainly that God took the cattle of their father and gave them to him. Moses meets his wife at a trough: “Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters: and they came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father's flock” (Exodus 2:16) — the shepherds drove them off, and the fugitive prince stood up for them. The pattern is worth noticing. Wells and troughs are where Isaac's bride, Jacob's wife, Moses' wife, and the Samaritan woman's Saviour are all met. Providence works at the ordinary places where people go for water.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a trough as a vessel, generally long and hollow, formed of wood or stone, to hold water for cattle to drink, or for other uses.
webster_full: TROUGH, n. [Sax. trog.] Any vessel, generally long and hollow, formed of wood or stone, to hold water for beasts to drink, or for other purposes.
TROUGH, n. A long hollow vessel in which bread is kneaded; a kneading-trough.
GUTTER, n. [Fr. gouttiere, from goutte, a drop.] A channel at the eaves of a house for conveying away the water; a channel or passage for water.
WATER, v.t. To supply with water; to let cattle drink; to lead to water.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals.
scriptures: Genesis 30:38
And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.
Genesis 30:41
And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.
Exodus 2:16
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters: and they came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.
Genesis 24:20
And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough, and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all his camels.
corruption_summary: Jacob's rods at the troughs are cited as evidence of prescientific superstition in the text, when the narrative itself assigns the increase to God and not to the sticks.
corruption_paragraphs: The peeled rods are a standing exhibit for the claim that Genesis records folk magic. Two things are usually left out. First, Genesis does not endorse the method; it reports what Jacob did, as it reports his deceptions elsewhere without commending them. Second, Jacob himself supplies the explanation two chapters on, telling Leah and Rachel that God had seen Laban's dealing and had taken away their father's cattle and given them to him — and that the instruction about the flocks came in a dream. The narrative credits providence and leaves the rods where it found them.

The wider lesson of the troughs is about where God works. Modern piety looks for Him at the unusual, and Scripture keeps staging His providence at the watering place: a servant praying for a sign over a camel's drink, a stone rolled from a well's mouth, seven daughters driven off by bullies, a woman at noon with a waterpot. The Lord Jesus began the greatest of those conversations by asking for a drink at an ordinary well. A Christian waiting for a burning bush may miss the trough.

roots_lines: Hebrew shoqeth (H8268) — a watering-trough; Genesis 24:20 and 30:38.
Hebrew rahat (H7298) — a trough or gutter; the gutters of Genesis 30:38, 41.
Hebrew ebus (H18) — a manger, feeding-trough; Proverbs 14:4, where the ox eats.
Hebrew beer (H875) — a well; the fixed setting of these meetings.
Greek phatne (G5336) — a manger; Luke 2:7, where the Lord was laid.

“Filled the troughs to water their father's flock” — and Moses met his wife.
“When they came to drink” — providence at the ordinary hour.

pos: n. (a parapet; the roof-rail God required on every Israelite house)
etymology: From Old French bataillier, to fortify. The KJV uses it both for a city's defensive parapet and, at Deuteronomy 22:8, for the low wall a householder must build around his flat roof — Hebrew maaqeh, a railing.
biblical_def: Among the laws of Deuteronomy is a building code, and it is a moral one: “When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence” (Deuteronomy 22:8). The flat roof was a room — people slept, dried grain, prayed, and ate there — so the law addresses an ordinary danger with an ordinary remedy. What is remarkable is the reason given. The householder who omits the rail brings blood upon his house, which means that a foreseeable death he did not prevent is charged to him. The sixth commandment therefore reaches past intent into negligence, and it reaches the man who is merely building. The word appears also of a city's defences, and there God claims the right to remove them: “Go ye up upon her walls, and destroy; but make not a full end: take away her battlements; for they are not the LORD'S” (Jeremiah 5:10). Zephaniah sounds the same alarm: “A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers” (Zephaniah 1:16). And Proverbs sends a man up to the roof the rail protects: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house” (Proverbs 21:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a battlement as a wall raised on a building with openings or embrasures, or a wall raised round the roof of a building as a fence or security.
webster_full: BATTLEMENT, n. A wall raised on a building with openings or embrasures, or elevations, originally for defense.
BATTLEMENT, n. A wall raised round the roof of a building, as a fence or security.
PARAPET, n. [It. parapetto, a breastwork.] A wall, rampart or elevation of earth, for covering soldiers from an enemy's shot; a breast-work.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house. In eastern countries the roofs were flat and used as places of resort.
NEGLIGENCE, n. Neglect; omission to do what ought to be done; want of due care or attention.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 22:8
When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence.
Jeremiah 5:10
Go ye up upon her walls, and destroy; but make not a full end: take away her battlements; for they are not the LORD'S.
Zephaniah 1:16
A day of the trumpet and alarm against the fenced cities, and against the high towers.
Proverbs 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
corruption_summary: The law is dismissed as antique safety regulation with nothing to say, when it is the sixth commandment applied to negligence and to the design of ordinary things.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglect is simply of the verse. Deuteronomy 22:8 is skipped as a quaint parapet ordinance, and it is one of the clearest statements in Scripture that guilt attaches to foreseeable harm a man declined to prevent. The principle to recover is that the commandment against killing governs the builder, the employer, the landlord, and the man who knows a thing is unsafe and says nothing — and that it governs them before anyone falls.

The second half of the verse is where the sharpness lies: that thou bring not blood upon thine house. The blood does not attach to the victim's misfortune or to the general run of accidents; it attaches to a house. Scripture's civil law repeatedly assigns responsibility this way, in the goring ox, the open pit, the unhedged roof. An age that resolves every such case into liability insurance has kept the payment and lost the category, and the category is the one that troubles a conscience before a death rather than after it.
roots_summary: Hebrew maaqeh (H4624), a parapet, railing; damim (H1818), blood, bloodguilt; natishah (H5189), a branch, battlement; gag (H1406), a roof.
roots_lines: Hebrew maaqeh (H4624) — a parapet; only Deuteronomy 22:8, rendered battlement.
Hebrew gag (H1406) — a flat roof; a living space, not merely a covering.
Hebrew damim (H1818) — bloods, bloodguilt; what a missing rail brings on a house.
Hebrew natishah (H5189) — a spreading branch, battlement; Jeremiah 5:10, taken away.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to kill, murder; the sixth commandment behind the building code.
usage: “Make a battlement for thy roof” — the sixth commandment, applied to carpentry.
“That thou bring not blood upon thine house” — guilt for a death not yet occurred.
“They are not the LORD'S” — defences God does not underwrite.

pos: n. (a smoke-hole; Hosea's figure for what Israel had become)
etymology: From Late Latin caminata, a room with a fireplace, from caminus, a furnace. The KJV uses it once, at Hosea 13:3, for the lattice or smoke-hole of an Israelite house — not a built stack, but the opening the smoke escaped through and vanished.
biblical_def: Hosea piles four figures on one another to say how little of Israel will remain: “Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney” (Hosea 13:3). Each is something real, visible, and gone within the hour, and the series moves from the merely brief to the actively swept away. The last is the sharpest, because smoke out of a smoke-hole is not carried off by a storm; it simply rises and is not. The occasion is idolatry — Ephraim had made molten images of his silver, and the prophet answers that a nation which worships what it manufactured will itself prove as substantial as its gods. The figure is drawn from the plainest fixtures of ordinary life: the chaff on the threshing-floor at winnowing time, as Ruth 3:2 has it — “And now is not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor” — and the locust swarm going in at the windows of Joel 2:9: “They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.” Scripture takes its images of judgment from the kitchen and the barn.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chimney as a body of brick or stone, containing a funnel or funnels, to convey smoke and other volatile matter through the roof of a building.
webster_full: CHIMNEY, n. [Fr. cheminee; L. caminus; Gr. a furnace.] In building, a body of brick or stone, erected in a building, containing a funnel or funnels, to convey smoke, and other volatile matter through the roof.
CHIMNEY, n. A fire-place; the lower part of the body of brick or stone which confines and conveys smoke.
SMOKE, n. [Sax. smoca.] The exhalation, visible vapor, or substance that escapes, or is expelled from a burning body.
CHAFF, n. [Sax. ceaf.] The husk, or dry calyx of corn and grasses. In Scripture, worthless matter; therefore, men who are worthless.
DEW, n. The water or moisture collected or deposited on or near the surface of the earth, during the night.
scriptures: Hosea 13:3
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.
Ruth 3:2
And now is not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor.
Joel 2:9
They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.
Proverbs 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
corruption_summary: Prophetic images of transience are read as poetic decoration, and the argument they carry — that what a people worships determines what that people becomes — is treated as rhetoric.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is interpretive. Hosea's four similes are heard as ornament, and they are an argument. Ephraim had made gods out of silver, and the prophet's claim is that a nation takes the substance of what it bows to; Psalm 115 states the same law plainly, that they that make idols are like unto them. The principle to recover is that the figures of the prophets carry the reasoning, and skipping them for the propositions loses the case.

The homeliness of the images is itself instructive. Smoke leaving a hole in the roof, chaff blowing off a threshing-floor, dew gone by nine in the morning — Hosea reaches for what a farmer sees every week, not for cosmic imagery. Judgment in Scripture is regularly described in the vocabulary of ordinary work, because the people addressed lived there. A preaching that must reach for the spectacular to make the last day feel real has a smaller vocabulary than the prophets did.

roots_lines: Hebrew arubbah (H699) — a lattice or opening; Hosea 13:3, rendered chimney; also the windows of heaven, Genesis 7:11.
Hebrew ashan (H6227) — smoke; the figure of what rises and is not.
Hebrew mots (H4671) — chaff; Psalm 1:4, the ungodly driven away.
Hebrew tal (H2919) — dew; Hosea 6:4, goodness that goeth early away.
Hebrew goren (H1637) — a threshing-floor; Ruth 3:2, where the winnowing is done.
usage: “As the smoke out of the chimney” — not swept away, simply gone.
“The early dew that passeth away” — visible, real, and finished by mid-morning.
“He winnoweth barley to night” — where the chaff figure comes from.

pos: n. (the threshing-floor; the place of a harvest that has failed)
etymology: From barn (Old English bere-aern, barley-house) + floor. The KJV uses the compound once, at 2 Kings 6:27, where the prophet's answer names the two places a starving city would normally find food — the threshing-floor and the winepress — and both are empty.
biblical_def: Samaria is under siege and a starving woman appeals to the king, who answers with a question that is half despair and half confession: “And he said, If the LORD do not help thee, whence shall I help thee? out of the barnfloor, or out of the winepress?” (2 Kings 6:27). The two places named are the ordinary sources — grain from the threshing-floor, wine from the press — and in a besieged city both are bare. The king is right that nothing but the LORD can help, and it is worth noting what he does next: he swears to kill Elisha for it. A true statement about God is not the same as faith in God. Scripture treats the threshing-floor as the appointed place of harvest and of meeting: “And now is not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor” (Ruth 3:2), where Ruth's redemption is settled. Hosea uses the same floor for judgment: “Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney” (Hosea 13:3). And Joel shows the siege from the invader's side: “They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief” (Joel 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a barn as a covered building for securing grain, hay and flax; and a barn-floor as the floor of a barn — in Scripture, the threshing-floor.
webster_full: BARN, n. [Sax. bern, from bere, barley, and ern, a place.] A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
BARN-FLOOR, n. The floor of a barn; the threshing-floor.
THRESHING-FLOOR, n. A floor or area, on which grain is beaten out.
WINEPRESS, n. A place where grapes are pressed, and the juice expressed.
FAMINE, n. [L. fames, hunger.] Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country or besieged place.
scriptures: 2 Kings 6:27
And he said, If the LORD do not help thee, whence shall I help thee? out of the barnfloor, or out of the winepress?
Ruth 3:2
And now is not Boaz of our kindred, with whose maidens thou wast? Behold, he winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor.
Hosea 13:3
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.
Joel 2:9
They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.
corruption_summary: A right statement about God's sole sufficiency is mistaken for faith, when the king who made it turned in the same hour to kill the prophet.
corruption_paragraphs: The king's sentence in 2 Kings 6:27 is theologically flawless. If the LORD does not help, no barnfloor and no winepress will. It is the sort of line that would be quoted approvingly in a sermon. Two verses later he vows that Elisha's head shall not stand on him this day, because he has concluded that the famine is the prophet's doing. Orthodoxy on the lips and rage at God's messenger in the heart can coexist in one man in one conversation, and Scripture puts them side by side so no one can plead the confession as evidence of the faith.

The barnfloor itself is worth holding onto. In Ruth it is where a redeemer is found; in Hosea it is where the chaff is separated; at Araunah's floor it becomes the site of the temple. A threshing-floor is the place where what is real is beaten out of what merely surrounded it, which is exactly what a famine does to a man's religion. The king was on that floor and did not know it.
roots_summary: Hebrew goren (H1637), a threshing-floor; yeqeb (H3342), a winepress; raab (H7458), famine; mots (H4671), chaff.
roots_lines: Hebrew goren (H1637) — a threshing-floor; rendered barnfloor at 2 Kings 6:27.
Hebrew yeqeb (H3342) — a winepress, the trough that receives the juice.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — hunger, famine; the siege condition of Samaria.
Hebrew zarah (H2219) — to winnow, scatter; Ruth 3:2, Boaz winnowing barley.
Hebrew mots (H4671) — chaff; what the floor exists to separate out.
usage: “Out of the barnfloor, or out of the winepress?” — the two ordinary sources, both empty.
“If the LORD do not help thee” — true, and not yet faith.
“He winnoweth barley to night” — the same floor, where a redeemer was found.

pos: n. (the burned debris of a ruined wall; what Nehemiah's builders had to move first)
etymology: From Anglo-French rubbous, broken stone. The KJV uses it in Nehemiah for Hebrew aphar, dust or rubble — the heaps of scorched stone left where Jerusalem's wall had been, which had to be cleared before a single new course could be laid.
biblical_def: Sanballat's mockery is a list of five questions, and the last one lands on the debris: “And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?” (Nehemiah 4:2). He is asking whether burned stone can be brought back to life, and the sneer is precise: the material itself looks beyond use. Halfway through the work, Judah says the same thing from the inside, and that is far more dangerous: “And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall” (Nehemiah 4:10). The enemy's taunt and the builders' discouragement agree word for word about the rubbish; they differ only in who is saying it. Nehemiah answers neither with an argument. He sets the people by families with a weapon in one hand and a tool in the other, and the wall goes up in fifty-two days. The stones were burned, and they were laid.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rubbish as fragments of buildings; broken or imperfect pieces of any structure; ruins; and, generally, any thing worthless.
webster_full: RUBBISH, n. Fragments of buildings; broken or imperfect pieces of any structure; ruins.
RUBBISH, n. Waste or rejected matter; any thing worthless.
RUBBISH, n. Mingled mass; confusion of materials.
RUIN, n. [L. ruina, from ruo, to fall.] Destruction; fall; overthrow; that change of any thing which destroys it, or entirely defeats its structure or purpose.
DEBRIS, n. Fragments; rubbish; ruins; a mass of broken material.
scriptures: Nehemiah 4:2

And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?
Nehemiah 4:10
And Judah said, The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed, and there is much rubbish; so that we are not able to build the wall.
Hosea 13:3
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.
Joel 2:9
They shall run to and fro in the city; they shall run upon the wall, they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief.
corruption_summary: Discouragement inside a work is treated as realism rather than as the enemy's argument arriving in a friendlier voice.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 4 puts the same assessment in two mouths eight verses apart. Sanballat says the stones are burned; Judah says there is much rubbish and we are not able. The facts were not in dispute — the strength of the bearers really had decayed, and the debris really was enormous. What made the second speech dangerous was not that it was false but that it was true and stopped there. A church can absorb a great deal of outside mockery and be halted entirely by an accurate internal report delivered with no reference to God.

The rubbish also refuses an easy spiritualizing. It had to be carried, load by load, by the same people who then laid the stones, and Nehemiah records no miracle that removed it. Restoration work in a life or a congregation usually begins with weeks of hauling burned material to a heap and nothing visible to show. Sanballat's sneer about reviving stones out of the heaps was answered by men with baskets, and the wall that went up was built of the burned stones.

Hebrew aremah (H6194) — a heap; the piles the builders had to clear.
Hebrew saraph (H8313) — to burn; the stones were scorched by the city's fall.
Hebrew sabbal (H5449) — a bearer of burdens; the men whose strength decayed.
Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, revive; Sanballat's sneer, revive the stones.
usage: “Revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish” — the mockery, and the actual plan.
“There is much rubbish; so that we are not able” — true, and it stopped there.
“The strength of the bearers of burdens is decayed” — the halfway report of every real work.

pos: n. pl. (soft limestone crushed to powder; Isaiah's figure for demolished altars)
etymology: From chalk (Latin calx, lime) + stone. Isaiah 27:9 uses it of the stones of an idolatrous altar beaten small — chalk being the softest of building stones, it shatters to dust and cannot be reassembled.
biblical_def: Isaiah states the terms on which Jacob's guilt is purged, and the evidence is rubble: “By this therefore shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit to take away his sin; when he maketh all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, the groves and images shall not stand up” (Isaiah 27:9). The choice of chalk is deliberate. A basalt altar knocked over can be set up again; chalkstone beaten in sunder becomes powder, and there is nothing left to raise. Repentance in this verse is measured by what cannot be reassembled afterward. The companion passage describes the same man's eyes: “And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, either the groves, or the images” (Isaiah 17:8). Note the phrases — the work of his hands, that which his fingers have made. An idol's whole absurdity is that the worshipper built it. The plain command runs all through the law: the high places are not to be regulated but broken, the groves cut down, the images burned. Isaiah does not offer reform of the altars. He offers powder.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chalk as a well known calcarious earth, of an opake white color, soft and admitting no polish — and chalk-stone, a mass or fragment of chalk.
webster_full: CHALK, n. [Sax. cealc; L. calx.] A well known calcarious earth, of an opake white color, soft, and admitting no polish.
CHALKSTONE, n. In medicine, a concretion; in general, a mass or fragment of chalk.
GROVE, n. In Scripture, the rendering of the Hebrew asherah, a wooden image or symbol set up beside an altar in idolatrous worship.
IMAGE, n. [L. imago.] A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; an idol.
ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other material, on which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity.
scriptures: Isaiah 27:9

By this therefore shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit to take away his sin; when he maketh all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, the groves and images shall not stand up.
Isaiah 17:8
And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, either the groves, or the images.
Nehemiah 4:2

And he spake before his brethren and the army of Samaria, and said, What do these feeble Jews? will they fortify themselves? will they sacrifice? will they make an end in a day? will they revive the stones out of the heaps of the rubbish which are burned?
Hosea 13:3
Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.
corruption_summary: Repentance is measured by regret rather than by demolition, and the idol is managed, relocated, or moderated instead of beaten to powder.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 27:9 sets an outward test on an inward work, and the test is destructive. The altar is not decommissioned or repurposed; its stones are beaten in sunder until they are chalk. A repentance that leaves the apparatus standing in the shed has not met Isaiah's description. The pattern in the historical books is the same: the faithful kings who merely failed to remove the high places are noted for it every time, and the ones commended pulled them down and burned the groves. Moderation of an idol is not a stage on the way to its destruction; it is usually the alternative to it.

Isaiah 17:8 names the reason an idol can be broken without loss, and it is the argument every idol cannot survive: the work of his hands…that which his fingers have made. A man's own product cannot save him. The modern forms are not carved, but they are still manufactured — a reputation, a portfolio, a system of self-management, a household ordered to keep one fear at bay. Each was built by the fingers that now depend on it, and each will shatter like chalk when it is struck. Better to strike it than to be under it when it goes.

Hebrew naphats (H5310) — to shatter, dash in pieces; beaten in sunder.
Hebrew asherah (H842) — the wooden cult symbol, rendered grove.
Hebrew chamman (H2553) — a sun-pillar or image; Isaiah 17:8, beside the groves.
Hebrew maaseh yadayw (H4639 + H3027) — the work of his hands; the whole case against an idol.
usage: “As chalkstones that are beaten in sunder” — powder, not a fallen altar.
“The groves and images shall not stand up” — nothing left to raise.
“That which his fingers have made” — the argument no idol survives.
